recipe: Call useDeferredValue at the top level of your component to get a deferred version of a value.
trigger_condition: You need to defer updating a part of your UI.
evidence: Call `useDeferredValue` at the top level of your component to get a deferred version of that value.

recipe: Pass primitive values (strings, numbers) or objects created outside of rendering to useDeferredValue; avoid creating a new object during rendering and immediately passing it, as it will differ on every render and cause unnecessary background re-renders.
trigger_condition: You are passing a value to useDeferredValue.
evidence: The values you pass to `useDeferredValue` should either be primitive values (like strings and numbers) or objects created outside of rendering. If you create a new object during rendering and immediately pass it to `useDeferredValue`, it will be different on every render, causing unnecessary background re-renders.

recipe: Pass a deferred version of a changing value (e.g. a search query) down to the component that performs expensive work, so it keeps showing stale results until the new results are ready instead of flashing a loading fallback.
trigger_condition: A child component does expensive work (like data fetching) and you want to avoid showing loading states on every keystroke.
evidence: A common alternative UI pattern is to *defer* updating the list of results and to keep showing the previous results until the new results are ready. Call `useDeferredValue` to pass a deferred version of the query down:

recipe: Do not rely on useDeferredValue to provide additional deferral when the update is already inside a Transition, because it will always return the new value and not spawn a deferred render.
trigger_condition: You are considering wrapping a useDeferredValue call inside a React Transition.
evidence: When an update is inside a Transition, `useDeferredValue` always returns the new `value` and does not spawn a deferred render, since the update is already deferred.

recipe: Remember that useDeferredValue does not prevent extra network requests; it only defers the re-render of the consuming component.
trigger_condition: You are using useDeferredValue with a data-fetching component and expect it to reduce the number of requests made.
evidence: `useDeferredValue` does not by itself prevent extra network requests.

recipe: Do not assume a fixed delay from useDeferredValue; the background re-render starts immediately after the original re-render completes and is interruptible by any new update to the value.
trigger_condition: You are timing or scheduling UI logic around the behavior of useDeferredValue.
evidence: There is no fixed delay caused by `useDeferredValue` itself. As soon as React finishes the original re-render, React will immediately start working on the background re-render with the new deferred value.

recipe: Add a visual indication (such as reducing opacity) when the deferred value lags behind the current value, so the user knows the displayed results are stale.
trigger_condition: When using useDeferredValue and the deferred value may be out of sync with the latest user input.
evidence: To make it more obvious to the user that the result list does not match the latest query, you can add a visual indication when the stale result list is displayed

recipe: Remember that useDeferredValue defers the display of results, not the underlying data fetching; a network request still fires per keystroke, but responses are cached so backspace is instant.
trigger_condition: When using useDeferredValue in combination with data fetching, to set correct expectations about what is and is not deferred.
evidence: Note that there is still a network request per each keystroke. What's being deferred here is displaying results (until they're ready), not the network requests themselves.

recipe: Use useDeferredValue instead of debouncing or throttling when you want interruptible re-renders that adapt to device speed without picking a fixed delay.
trigger_condition: You are optimizing a re-render that should be interruptible and scale with the user's device performance.
evidence: Unlike debouncing or throttling, it doesn't require choosing any fixed delay.

recipe: Use debouncing or throttling when the work you're optimizing doesn't happen during rendering, such as reducing the number of network requests.
trigger_condition: You need to limit side effects like network calls rather than re-renders.
evidence: If the work you're optimizing doesn't happen during rendering, debouncing and throttling are still useful. For example, they can let you fire fewer network requests.

recipe: Combine useDeferredValue with debouncing or throttling when you need both interruptible re-renders and reduced frequency of side effects.
trigger_condition: Your component has both expensive re-renders and side effects (e.g. network calls) that need different optimization strategies.
evidence: You can also use these techniques together.
